blocks.text: 1. The Reset Gate

blocks.alt: The previous hidden state feeds the reset gate to produce filtered past information

blocks.text: The Update Gate, the previous topic, decided how much of the previous hidden state to keep versus replace. The Reset Gate is GRU's second and final gate, explored in full depth throughout this topic.
It decides how much of the previous hidden state to genuinely ignore when computing new candidate values, a genuinely important complementary mechanism covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Preview

This connects back to two gates instead of three, already covered in GRU Architecture. The reset gate was genuinely introduced there as the second of GRU's two gates, briefly described in that earlier topic.
This topic genuinely completes the full, dedicated treatment of both gates covered throughout this module, closing out this module's exploration of GRU's own gating mechanism.
3. Where The Reset Gate Fits

blocks.alt: The reset gate feeds into the candidate hidden state

blocks.text: This connects back to the candidate values, already covered in The Input Gate and The Update Gate. The reset gate genuinely acts before the candidate values, already covered, even get computed.

It controls how much of the past genuinely influences that new candidate computation itself, a genuinely earlier point in the overall update process than the update gate's own role already covered in the previous topic.

blocks.text: 4. The Core Operation

The reset gate's genuinely core operation connects back to the Sigmoid gating mechanism, already covered in LSTM Architecture. Compute a Sigmoid value from the current input and previous hidden state, the exact same familiar pattern.

This directly reuses the exact same gating computation already covered throughout every gate in this module, keeping the reset gate's own design genuinely consistent with everything already covered so far.
5. Applying The Reset

blocks.alt: The reset gate value multiplies the previous hidden state to produce a filtered hidden state

blocks.text: This connects back to element-wise multiplication, already covered throughout the forget and input gates. Multiply the genuinely previous hidden state by the reset gate's own value before computing the new candidate values.

This genuinely reduces the past's influence exactly where the network decides it is genuinely less relevant, directly shaping what information the candidate computation, already covered, actually gets to see.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This positioning, already covered in this topic, before the candidate computation rather than after it, is exactly what distinguishes the reset gate's own role from the update gate's own role already covered in the previous topic.

blocks.text: 6. When Information Should Genuinely Be Ignored

blocks.alt: A new segment starting causes the reset gate to clear the past

blocks.text: A genuinely important, real practical scenario connects back to the temporal dependency concept, already covered in Sequence Data. Starting a genuinely new topic or sentence often means the immediately prior context genuinely matters less.

The reset gate, already covered throughout this topic, gives the network a genuinely learned, deliberate way to recognize and act on exactly this kind of genuinely real, practical shift in relevant context.
7. Reset Versus Update: A Direct Contrast

blocks.alt: The reset gate decides how much past to use while the update gate decides how much to keep

blocks.text: This connects back to the update gate, already covered in its own topic. The update gate controls the genuinely final blend of old and new; the reset gate controls how the new candidate itself gets computed.

These are two genuinely distinct, complementary roles working together throughout every single time step, together forming the complete two-gate design already covered generally throughout GRU Architecture.

blocks.text: 8. The Full GRU Equation, Recapped

blocks.alt: The reset gate and update gate together produce the new hidden state

blocks.text: This connects back to the interpolation formula, already covered in The Update Gate. Together, the reset gate and update gate genuinely form GRU's complete hidden state update.

This is the full picture already assembled piece by piece across these final two topics of this module, bringing together everything covered throughout LSTM & GRU into GRU's own complete, working mechanism.
9. Recognizing Why The Reset Gate Is Genuinely Essential

blocks.alt: Needing to ignore past context points toward the reset gate

blocks.text: This connects back to genuinely shifting context within a sequence, already covered in this topic. The reset gate, already covered in this topic, directly lets the network discount genuinely stale prior context.
Completing GRU's own two-gate design, already covered throughout this module, is another genuine case where the reset gate, already covered, is genuinely the final piece alongside the update gate.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely complete GRU time step, using both the reset gate and update gate together, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic and the previous one.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
hidden_size = 4

def gru_step(x_t, h_prev, rng):
    # already covered as the core operation in both this topic and the previous one
    reset_gate = sigmoid(rng.normal(size=hidden_size) * 0.5)   # already covered as the reset gate in this topic
    update_gate = sigmoid(rng.normal(size=hidden_size) * 0.5)  # already covered as the update gate in the previous topic

    # already covered as applying the reset in this topic: reducing the past's influence before computing candidates
    reset_hidden = reset_gate * h_prev
    candidate = np.tanh(rng.normal(size=hidden_size) * 0.3 + reset_hidden)

    # already covered as the interpolation formula in the previous topic
    h_t = update_gate * h_prev + (1 - update_gate) * candidate
    return h_t

hidden_state = np.zeros(hidden_size)
sequence = [rng.normal(size=hidden_size) for _ in range(4)]

for t, x_t in enumerate(sequence):
    hidden_state = gru_step(x_t, hidden_state, rng)
    print(f"Time step {t}: hidden state = {np.round(hidden_state, 3)}")

print("\nThis full step used both the reset gate and update gate together, already covered throughout this topic and the previous one")

blocks.text: 11. LSTM & GRU: Module Complete

items: The reset gate decides how much of the previous hidden state to ignore for new candidate values.
It acts before the candidate values get computed, an earlier point than the update gate's own role.
It computes a Sigmoid value from the current input and previous hidden state, like every other gate.
It multiplies into the previous hidden state before candidate computation, reducing the past's influence.
It helps the network recognize shifts in relevant context, like starting a new topic or sentence.
The update gate controls the final blend; the reset gate controls how the candidate itself gets computed.
Together, these two gates form GRU's complete hidden state update.
